system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

For every objection also fill `uae_basis`: if one of the UAE clauses shown (ids starting with ITU-UAE:, TDRA-,
UAE-, DXB-) speaks to this issue, set status "cites_uae" with its id and a word-for-word quote; otherwise set
status "none_applies" with empty ref and quote. Say "none_applies" honestly: it tells the regulator where UAE
texts are silent.

Emergency messages should be sent out to users in their own language but when not practicable, then in the language of the message originator. data.summary: The Arabic adds a sea-wave height claim (more than 6 feet) that is not in the English, and renders the wind figure as 'more than 50 km/h' where the English says 'might exceed 50 km/h'. The English also gives no protective action beyond 'take appropriate action', and the Arabic matches that vagueness. How the Arabic was produced is unknown, so a named Arabic reader must check it.

objections.issue: The Arabic says sea waves will rise to more than 6 feet (وارتفاع الأمواج البحرية لأكثر من 6 أقدام). The English only says 'leading to rough sea' and gives no wave height. This is a number added in the Arabic with no source in the English. Either the English is incomplete or the Arabic is wrong.
objections.fix: Delete the wave-height figure from the Arabic and use a plain equivalent of 'rough sea' (مما يؤدي إلى اضطراب البحر). If the 6-foot figure is a real forecast, the issuing authority must confirm it and add it to the English too.

evidence.quote: وارتفاع الأمواج البحرية ﻷكثر من 6 أقدام

objections.issue: The wind speed is stated more firmly in the Arabic than in the English. 'Might exceed 50 km/h' becomes 'may reach a speed of more than 50 km/h' (قد تصل سرعتها إلى أكثر من ٥٠), which is clumsy. The Arabic also mixes Arabic-Indic digits (٥٠) with Western digits (6) in the same text, which is inconsistent. 'Fresh winds' is rendered as 'wind activity' (نشاط في الرياح), which is not the same meaning.
objections.fix: Use 'رياح قوية/منعشة قد تتجاوز سرعتها 50 كم/ساعة' and use one digit style throughout.

no_basis.concern: The protective action ('Take appropriate action' / اتخاذ التدابير اللازمة) is generic in both languages. It is consistent between them, but it does not tell the public what to do. This is outside Arabic-English fidelity.
